newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr bulls find voice as rate cloud lifts.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr bulls find voice as rate cloud lifts.

text.p: The Australian dollar breezed through a Reserve Bank rate cut to finish a cent higher Wednesday as bulls finally scented an end to policy uncertainty.

The 0.5 point cut in official cash rates to 5.0 percent came a little earlier than most had expected, but it was a testament to how completely discounted the move was that the dollar wobbled only briefly before recovering.
"It feels fundamentally bid now," said one at a Melbourne bank. "I think London and New York will see this as a buying opportunity and take the Aussie above the figure (75 cents)."

By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had romped to US$0.7462/67, its best local close in three weeks, having briefly dipped 1/2 cent to US$0.7395 immediately after the RBA announcement hit dealing screens.
This was a nonchalant performance given it ended Tuesday at US$0.7360/65 and the market had been confidently assuming the RBA would not move before its monthly board meeting next week.

While slightly baffled by the timing, dealers said the event itself had been anticipated almost since the last easing on May 23. The A$ had fallen from 78 cents in the intervening period to reflect this expectation, leaving much of the market short.

It was these shorts which were squeezed Tuesday when a burst of buying from several sources, including a Swiss bank, a U.S. fund and a Canadian corporate, breached key levels at US$0.7380, US$0.7420 and US$0.7470 sparking panic stop loss bids.
Where the currency went now depended largely on whether today's move really was the last in the easing cycle, as most analysts were predicting.

"The accumulated rate cuts in the pipeline plus the, relative, softness of the dollar point to a pronounced pickup in economic growth that would seem to rule out the need for further cuts," said Stephen Roberts, an economist at UBS Australia.
The bank has eased by a total 250 basis points since the cycle began, which oddly enough was almost exactly a year ago today, bringing the official rate down to a three year trough.
Market rates have come down even further as fierce banking competition drove mortgage rates to 30 year lows.

Analysts thought this amount of monetary adrenaline was bound to have an effect on growth eventually, but some cautioned the real side of the economy would have to show clear signs of life soon for speculation of a sixth easing to be avoided.
"We recommend clients take the view we are in an easing cycle until the data says otherwise," said economist Tony Meer.

"As we expect economic and employment growth to remain softer than desired over the remainder of 1997, we expect the balance of risks to be for a further 50 basis point cut in three to four months time," said Meer at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Data on the housing market today illustrated how hard it was to rule out another easing entirely. Building approvals fell 4.5 percent against forecasts of a 1.5 percent dip and trend growth turned negative for the first time in more than a year.
If June retail sales out Thursday and the crucial jobs figures for July next week disappointed as well, speculation of a further cut could come in a hurry.
For now, the futures market seemed inclined to take the steady policy line and the December 90 bank bill contract settled at 95.07, implying a rate of 4.93 percent.

The chart outlook had also improved following the break of last week's US$0.7440 high which suggested the recent 18-month low of US$0.7310 was the bottom of its downtrend. A breach of US$0.7550 would confirm it and allow a rally to US$0.7680.

It was broadly firmer on the crosses as heavy short covering on AUD/yen positions lifted it to 88.74/84 from 86.58/68. It leapt to 5-1/2 year highs on the mark around 1.3760 and surged to 58.3 in trade weighted terms from 57.6. -- 61-2 9373 1800
